summary_html: Child achieves **permanency through legal guardianship** or kinship care. Federal programs provide funding parity with adoption for approved relatives.

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a minor over fourteen who nominates a relative as guardian does not thereby permit a court to divest his fit, non-offending biological mother of custody, although the child may be entitled to visitation with the grandmother.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading WV case on contested guardianship as permanency against a biological parent.
key_cases.quote: A court may not divest Gina H., Antonio's biological mother, of her custodial rights simply because Carol G. would be a "fit" guardian

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming denial of a non-parent guardianship petition, the Court held that a court appointing a guardian under W. Va. Code § 44-10-3 must give priority to the child's mother or father, and that a family court presented with abuse and neglect allegations in a guardianship petition must refer the matter under Rule 48a(a).
key_cases.relevance: It is the governing framework for guardianship as a permanency route in West Virginia.
key_cases.quote: In appointing a guardian, the court shall give priority to the minor's mother or father

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Vacating and remanding, the Court held that a circuit court denying placement with a grandparent must enter detailed findings showing it considered the statutory grandparent preference and determined, on the whole record, that the preference was overcome by the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: Permanency through kinship cannot be rejected in a conclusory order.
key_cases.quote: in denying grandparent placement the circuit court must make detailed findings of fact and conclusions of law demonstrating that it considered the grandparent preference

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a parent who validly relinquished her parental rights lost her status as a 'parent' and therefore lacked standing to move under W. Va. Code § 49-6-6 for modification of the child's disposition, because a final termination order completely severs the parent-child relationship.
key_cases.relevance: It explains why a terminated parent cannot later contest a guardianship or permanency disposition as a 'parent.'
key_cases.quote: a final order terminating a person's parental rights, as the result of either an involuntary termination or a voluntary relinquishment of parental rights, completely severs the parent-child relationship

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Holding that the lower tribunals abused their discretion by failing to apply the statutory grandparent preference, the Court remanded with directions that the child be placed with his paternal grandparents for adoption following a gradual transition of custody.
key_cases.relevance: It governs when kinship placement must be chosen over a non-relative foster home as the child's permanent home, and requires the agency to actually assist relatives in developing a permanency plan.
key_cases.quote: the preference for grandparent placement may be overcome only where the record reviewed in its entirety establishes that such placement is not in the best interests of the child

key_cases.case_name: Elmer Jimmy S. v. Kenneth B.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming denial of the paternal grandparents' visitation petition, the Court held that although circuit courts have jurisdiction to consider grandparent visitation even after the related parent's rights are terminated, the terminated parent cannot satisfy the statute's 'noncustodial parent' requirement because the law no longer recognizes him as a parent.
key_cases.relevance: It is the authority on which In re Cesar L. expressly builds its syllabus point: once rights are terminated the law no longer recognizes that individual as a 'parent,' which controls who may claim parental status in a later guardianship, visitation or permanency dispute.
key_cases.quote: Thus, the non-parent whose parental rights have been terminated could not then be deemed a "noncustodial parent."
